demo-scene-kit-api-usedemo-scene-kit-integration0 of 2 (critical)failThe Talk boundary uses the kit correctly. The shared ReferenceScene mostly does too. But it bypasses and duplicates the kit&#39;s node mechanism for five entities. The tray, verify, socket and modify entities are raw `motion.div layout layoutId` elements. The conversation arrow is a hand-written `motion.svg layout layoutId` with its own arrow path. The kit already supplies these through `Node` (shared.tsx) and `Arrow`. `Node` adds the `LAYOUT_T` transition and `data-presentation-node`. `Arrow` adds the same arrow path. The raw elements skip both, so they re-implement the shared layout mechanism and lose the kit&#39;s transition timing.Talk.tsx renders `&lt;Presentation steps={STEPS} title=... initialMode=&quot;browse&quot; /&gt;`, so orchestration goes through the kit. | ReferenceScene.tsx uses kit `SceneLayer`, `Box`, `Label`, `Frame`, `Emphasis` and `SymbolChip` for most entities. | ReferenceScene.tsx hand-rolls `motion.svg ... layoutId={E.conversation}`, with its own arrow path, instead of the kit `Arrow`. | ReferenceScene.tsx hand-rolls `motion.div layout layoutId={E.tray}`, `E.verify`, `E.socket` and `E.modify` instead of `Box`, `Frame` or `Label`. | shared.tsx `Node` applies `transition={{ duration: LAYOUT_T }}` and `data-presentation-node`; the raw elements apply neither. | judging basis: majority-fail | src/presentations/how-to-make-a-presentation/Talk.tsx | src/presentations/how-to-make-a-presentation/ReferenceScene.tsx | src/presentation-kit/nodes/shared.tsx | src/presentation-kit/nodes/Arrow.tsx | src/presentation-kit/Presentation.tsx
demo-stable-identity-and-groupingdemo-identity-and-grouping2 of 2 (critical)passGrouping: steps/index.tsx builds all nine steps from one outline map, each with Scene: ReferenceScene and groupKey: &#39;reference-scene&#39;. Stage calls sceneTransitionKey, which uses resolveGroup. That matches adjacent steps with the same groupKey and Scene and returns the same key, `group:reference-scene:0`, for all nine. There is no npm or npx wrapper, so the child being killed is the preview server process. That spawn, the bounded readiness loop, `chromium.launch`, and every check sit inside one `try`. Its `finally` closes the browser and, if `preview.exitCode === null`, sends SIGTERM. It then awaits `Promise.race([new Promise(r =&gt; preview.once(&#39;exit&#39;, r)), delay(3000)])` and sends SIGKILL if the server is still running. The failing-check path also reaches that `finally`. In both verify copies, `fail` is defined as `function fail(phase, message) { throw new Error(...) }` (verify.mjs line 10, verify-presentation.mjs line 16). It throws and never calls process.exit, so readiness failure, readiness timeout and every failing render check unwind through the `finally`. The `.catch(() =&gt; fail(...))` calls on `waitForFunction` rethrow inside the awaited promise, so they propagate the same way. The top-level callers catch the error and set `process.exitCode = 1`, which also never calls process.exit, so cleanup finishes before the script exits. Success falls through to the `finally` as well. The bootstrap copies match the repository copies line for line. Judges A and B are consistent with this source. Lines 116-130: catch …","The bootstrap template copies skills/presentation/templates/bootstrap/scripts/{verify.mjs, verify-presentation.mjs, inspect-presentation.mjs} match the repository copies line for line, including the …","quoted lines: scripts/verify-presentation.mjs:1-112","quoted lines: scripts/verify.mjs:1-111","quoted lines: scripts/inspect-presentation.mjs:1-130","quoted lines: skills/presentation/templates/bootstrap/scripts/verify-presentation.mjs:1-112","quoted lines: skills/presentation/templates/bootstrap/scripts/verify.mjs:1-111","quoted lines: skills/presentation/templates/bootstrap/scripts/inspect-presentation.mjs:1-130","decider ruling: pass, confirmed by the closed-world span audit"]}},"rationale":"Every exit path in all six copies (repository and bootstrap template copies of verify.mjs, verify-presentation.mjs and inspect-presentation.mjs) terminates the preview server and awaits its exit. There is no npm or npx wrapper, so the child being killed is the preview server process. That spawn, the bounded readiness loop, `chromium.launch`, and every check sit inside one `try`. Its `finally` closes the browser and, if `preview.exitCode === null`, sends SIGTERM. It then awaits `Promise.race([new Promise(r =&gt; preview.once(&#39;exit&#39;, r)), delay(3000)])` and sends SIGKILL if the server is still running. The failing-check path also reaches that `finally`. In both verify copies, `fail` is defined as `function fail(phase, message) { throw new Error(...) }` (verify.mjs line 10, verify-presentation.mjs line 16). It throws and never calls process.exit, so readiness failure, readiness timeout and every failing render check unwind through the `finally`. The `.catch(() =&gt; fail(...))` calls on `waitForFunction` rethrow inside the awaited promise, so they propagate the same way. The top-level callers catch the error and set `process.exitCode = 1`, which also never calls process.exit, so cleanup finishes before the script exits. In inspect, every failure inside the try is a literal `throw`, and the catch sets `process.exitCode = 1` before the `finally` runs. The `process.exit` calls at inspect lines 20, 21 and 25 happen before the preview is spawned at line 45, so no preview exists yet on those paths. A browser launch failure (`chromium.launch` at verify.mjs:48, verify-presentation.mjs:57, inspect:64) happens after the spawn and inside the try, so it reaches the same cleanup. Success falls through to the `finally` as well. The bootstrap copies match the repository copies line for line. Judges A and B are consistent with this source. Judge C points to the SIGINT/SIGTERM interrupt handler, which calls process.exit(130) without awaiting the preview&#39;s exit. The criterion&#39;s guidance lists the exit paths to trace as success, a failing check, a browser launch failure, and an error after the preview started; signal interruption is not among them, so it does not decide the requirement. Even on that path the handler sends SIGTERM to the vite server itself, not to a wrapper. Judge C&#39;s second point is that the SIGKILL fallback is not awaited. Each runs `spawn(process.execPath, [node_modules/vite/bin/vite.js, &#39;preview&#39;, ...])`, so the child process is the Vite server itself, not an npm or npx wrapper. The spawn, the readiness wait, `chromium.launch` and every check all sit inside one `try`. Its `finally` closes the browser. If the preview is still running, it sends SIGTERM, waits for the preview&#39;s &#39;exit&#39; event (up to 3 seconds), and sends SIGKILL if the process is still alive. Success, a failing check (`fail()` throws), a browser launch failure and any error after the preview started all pass through that `finally`. The bootstrap copies have the same lines at the same line numbers. I agree with Judges A and B. Judge C&#39;s first reason is the SIGINT/SIGTERM interrupt handler, which calls `process.exit(130)` without waiting for the preview to exit. Neither the requirement nor its guidance names a signal interrupt as an exit path; they name success, a failing check, a browser launch failure and an error after start. Judge C&#39;s second reason is that the SIGKILL fallback is not awaited. That fallback runs only after the awaited SIGTERM wait times out, and SIGKILL cannot be caught or ignored, so the server process itself is still terminated. Neither reason shows a named exit path leaving the preview running.","evidence":["scripts/verify.mjs renderSample: the preview is spawned at line 34 inside `try` (line 33), and `chromium.launch` follows at line 48. of verify.mjs, verify-presentation.mjs and inspect-presentation.mjs) terminates the preview server and awaits its exit. Each script starts the server itself with `spawn(process.execPath, [&lt;root&gt;/node_modules/vite/bin/vite.js, &#39;preview&#39;, ...])`. There is no npm or npx wrapper, so the child being killed is the preview server process. That spawn, the bounded readiness loop, `chromium.launch`, and every check sit inside one `try`. Its `finally` closes the browser and, if `preview.exitCode === null`, sends SIGTERM. It then awaits `Promise.race([new Promise(r =&gt; preview.once(&#39;exit&#39;, r)), delay(3000)])` and sends SIGKILL if the server is still running. The failing-check path also reaches that `finally`. In both verify copies, `fail` is defined as `function fail(phase, message) { throw new Error(...) }` (verify.mjs line 10, verify-presentation.mjs line 16). It throws and never calls process.exit, so readiness failure, readiness timeout and every failing render check unwind through the `finally`. The `.catch(() =&gt; fail(...))` calls on `waitForFunction` rethrow inside the awaited promise, so they propagate the same way. The top-level callers catch the error and set `process.exitCode = 1`, which also never calls process.exit, so cleanup finishes before the script exits. In inspect, every failure inside the try is a literal `throw`, and the catch sets `process.exitCode = 1` before the `finally` runs. The `process.exit` calls at inspect lines 20, 21 and 25 happen before the preview is spawned at line 45, so no preview exists yet on those paths. A browser launch failure (`chromium.launch` at verify.mjs:48, verify-presentation.mjs:57, inspect:64) happens after the spawn and inside the try, so it reaches the same cleanup. Success falls through to the `finally` as well. The bootstrap copies match the repository copies line for line. Judges A and B are consistent with this source. Judge C points to the SIGINT/SIGTERM interrupt handler, which calls process.exit(130) without awaiting the preview&#39;s exit. The criterion&#39;s guidance lists the exit paths to trace as success, a failing check, a browser launch failure, and an error after the preview started; signal interruption is not among them, so it does not decide the requirement. Even on that path the handler sends SIGTERM to the vite server itself, not to a wrapper. Judge C&#39;s second point is that the SIGKILL fallback is not awaited. The signal-interrupt handler (process.exit(130)) is not one of the exit paths the guidance names, and it still sends SIGTERM to the Vite server directly.
